items.s: No marketing of the securities and no offers or sales to the public may occur.
items.w: Before the registration statement is filed, the offering legally does not exist, so no marketing is allowed.

items.s: A road show may be held to present the offering to prospective investors.
items.w: Road shows promote the deal after filing, while the SEC reviews the registration statement for disclosure.

items.s: Investors may be asked for non-binding indications of interest.
items.w: Underwriters collect IOIs after filing to gauge demand and help determine where to price the issue.

items.s: The period lasts until the registration statement is filed with the SEC.
items.w: The pre-filing or quiet period ends at filing, which is when the cooling-off period begins.

items.s: A preliminary prospectus without the final price may be distributed.
items.w: The red herring is distributed during the cooling-off period and omits the offer price and share count.

items.s: The bake-off, the mandate and due diligence on the S-1 take place here.
items.w: The pitch, engagement letter and S-1 preparation all occur before the registration statement is filed.

items.s: Subject to a six-month holding period when the issuer is a reporting company.
items.w: Restricted stock has never been registered, so Rule 144 requires holding it six months before resale.

items.s: Sales are capped at the greater of 1% of outstanding shares or average weekly volume.
items.w: The volume limit applies to affiliates selling control stock over any 90-day period.

items.s: Held by an officer, a director or an owner of more than 10% of voting shares.
items.w: Control stock is defined by the holder being an affiliate or corporate insider of the issuer.

items.s: Acquired through a private placement, an employee benefit plan or as seed capital.
items.w: Restricted stock arises from unregistered acquisitions such as private placements and compensation or start-up funding.

items.s: Requires adequate current public information about the issuer before the sale.
items.w: Restricted stock can only be resold under Rule 144 when the issuer is a public reporting company.

items.s: The holder files Form 144 before selling unless sales stay at or below $50,000 over three months.
items.w: Insiders must file Form 144 before selling control shares in the open market, subject to that dollar threshold.

items.s: The syndicate buys the whole issue from the issuer and resells it to the public.
items.w: Underwriters purchase all shares, taking financial liability for whatever they cannot resell.

items.s: Underwriters act as agents and bear no financial liability for unsold securities.
items.w: In best efforts the underwriter only attempts to sell and has no obligation to buy unsold shares.

items.s: A standby commitment used with a rights offering is a type of this underwriting.
items.w: A standby commitment is a firm commitment under which underwriters buy shares existing shareholders do not subscribe to.

items.s: All-or-none and mini-max arrangements are forms of this underwriting.
items.w: All-or-none and mini-max are both variations of best efforts that can cancel a deal if targets are missed.

items.s: Usually used for private placements and offerings of risky securities.
items.w: Best efforts suits riskier deals where underwriters will not take on the risk of unsold securities.

items.s: Unsold shares are distributed among the members of the syndicate.
items.w: Syndicate members share financial responsibility for any shares left unsold in a firm commitment.

items.s: An already-public issuer sells additional stock to the public after its IPO.
items.w: A follow-on is any later offering by an issuer that already has publicly traded securities.

items.s: All proceeds belong to existing shareholders who sell their own shares.
items.w: In a secondary offering the selling shareholders receive the proceeds, not the issuing company.

items.s: No new shares are created, so the issuer’s net worth is unchanged.
items.w: Because only existing shares are sold, the company’s net worth stays the same in a secondary offering.

items.s: The label depends on the issuer already having publicly traded securities.
items.w: Follow-on versus IPO turns on whether the issuer is already public, not on who receives the proceeds.

items.s: Apple, already public, issues more stock to raise capital for the company.
items.w: A publicly traded company doing another stock offering is the book’s example of a follow-on.

items.s: A founder and a venture firm sell positions while the company sells no shares.
items.w: A registration covering only existing shareholders’ shares is identified in the prospectus as a secondary offering.

items.s: Governs private placements and defines accredited investors.
items.w: Regulation D is the rule that governs private placements and the types of permitted investors.

items.s: Permits resale of unregistered securities freely among qualified institutional buyers.
items.w: Rule 144A lets QIBs trade unregistered securities among themselves, increasing institutional resale liquidity.

items.s: Generally allows a maximum of 35 non-accredited investors to participate.
items.w: Private placements under Regulation D generally permit up to 35 non-accredited investors alongside unlimited accredited ones.

items.s: A broker-dealer with a $10 million securities portfolio can qualify as a buyer.
items.w: Broker-dealers with at least $10 million in securities are QIBs, versus $100 million for other institutions.

items.s: An individual with a net worth of $1 million excluding the primary residence qualifies.
items.w: That net worth test defines an accredited investor, not a qualified institutional buyer.

items.s: An institution must manage at least $100 million in securities to qualify.
items.w: QIB status requires managing a securities portfolio of at least $100 million, a far higher bar than accredited status.
